transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Lunaris Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Infra), Sofia Morales (Product), Ahmed Khan (SRE)

Summary: quick run through of benchmark spreadsheet, discuss caching and batching numbers, align on what to test next for latency-sensitive paths.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll do a 2 minute agenda - bench review, caching numbers, batching tradeoffs, and then next steps.
[00:15] Priya: sounds good, we want to focus on per-unit economics - tokens per dollar, and latency for our customer-facing widgets.
[00:30] Ethan: quick context - last week we ran two sets: hosted API baseline and a Redwood dedicated profile with quantized model. We also tested prefix / KV cache for repeated prompts.
[00:45] Tom: quick question, when you say quantized, is that int8 or the new q4_0-ish? i know names are fuzzy in the transcript but we need to know CPU/GPU memory.
[01:05] Ethan: it was the q4-1 path we used for the dedicated run — sorry, i might have said q4-0 earlier — baseline was fp16 on hosted.
[01:25] Priya: what were the tokens/sec numbers? our SLO needs 2000 tokens/sec aggregate for 99th p50? sorry i mean p95 for our widget.
[01:40] Ethan: okay so for the sample prompt mix you shared, hosted baseline (fp16) averaged ~1,100 tokens/sec on a single shared slot (this is from our sample with 1.2k average prompt length), dedicated q4 run was about 1,850 tokens/sec. With dynamic batching turned on we saw bursts to ~2,300 tokens/sec but tail latency increased — p95 latency jumped from ~140ms to ~370ms for some long sequences.
[02:15] Sofia: that's notable. and caching? i remember you said prefix cache gave big savings on repeated prompts.
[02:25] Ethan: yes, with prefix (KV) cache enabled we saw token savings of ~30% overall on the sample mix; on routes with high repetition the savings hit 45%. That translated to lower effective $/1k tokens because fewer tokens were generated end-to-end.
[02:45] Ahmed: is that counting tokenization differences? sometimes repeated short tokens can inflate counts.
[02:55] Liam: good call; we normalized by BPE token counts used in your model and included bpe normalization in the sheet. there was some noise but overall the percent savings is stable.
[03:15] Priya: can you put that into tokens/sec per dollar? that's what our finance team will ask.
[03:25] Ethan: sure — rough numbers from the pilot: hosted baseline cost profile gave about 0.9 tokens/sec per dollar (this is unitized for your sample mix and the shared-host pricing). Dedicated quantized nodes improved that to ~2.1 tokens/sec per dollar. With caching applied, effective tokens/sec per dollar for dedicated climbed to ~3.0 tokens/sec per dollar on high-repeat routes.
[03:55] Priya: those look promising. what's the caveat?
[04:00] Ethan: the caveat is tail latency — batching improves aggregate throughput and cost but can hurt P95 if you let batch windows get too large. Also cache hits help cost but are only effective when prompts repeat or when prefix patterns are stable; for highly diverse prompts cache benefit drops.
[04:20] Tom: for our latency critical widget we can't accept p95 > 250ms. so the dedicated q4 numbers with batching might not meet that unless we tune batch sizes or reserve dedicated low-latency nodes.
[04:35] Maya: yep, that's exactly the tradeoff — dedicated reserved slots give predictable latency SLOs at higher commit cost vs hosted where you get cheaper but variable tail. We should test dedicated nodes with tight batching thresholds and smaller worker sizes.
[04:55] Priya: what's the expected cost delta if we go dedicated with lower latency tuning?
[05:05] Ethan: rough delta — if you reserve 2x dedicated low-latency nodes and cap batching windows to 20ms, you reduce throughput by ~20% vs the high-batch runs, so tokens/sec per dollar drops from 2.1 to about 1.6 for dedicated. But p95 improves to ~120-180ms depending on prompt length.
[05:30] Sofia: can we mix routes? like critical widget on dedicated low-latency and background batch jobs on high-throughput dedicated or hosted?
[05:40] Maya: absolutely — smart routing is what we recommend: route latency-sensitive routes to dedicated low-latency instances, and spillover or non-critical calls to cheaper pools. Redwood supports policy-based routing and can fallback automatically.
[05:55] Priya: inventory of questions from our side: 1) exact tokens/sec/$ calculation, 2) how caching interacts with RBAC/data privacy (do caches store user data?), 3) how we can test dedicated latency in our VPC.
[06:15] Ethan: quick answers — 1) we'll share the spreadsheet with math and per-route calc, 2) KV cache can be configured per-customer and can be disabled; cached items are kept in encrypted memory and not persisted unless you opt-in, and indexes are isolated per-tenant on dedicated, 3) for VPC tests we need peering info; Tom if you can enable a test peering we'll spin up a dedicated node in the same region and run the latency suite.
[06:45] Tom: we can do peering, i'll get the test account details to you.
[06:50] Ahmed: small note — does the cache use KMS? we need to know about key management.
[06:55] Ethan: yes, we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) on Private deployments and can integrate with your KMS for encryption at rest; for hosted cache we use our managed KMS but enterprise customers can request customer KMS for logs/keys on private/dedicated.
[07:15] Priya: any concerns about our prompt diversity? the cache benefit may be lower than you saw in your sample runs.
[07:25] Liam: totally, that's why we asked for a 3-week sample prompt mix. once we run the same bench with your real distribution we'll have a better projection of cache hit rates and unit economics.
[07:40] Maya: ok next steps recap — Ethan will run a batch + cache bench with dedicated low-latency cap config and share the sheet; Maya will send updated pricing; Lunaris will provide prompt samples and enable peering.
[07:55] Priya: timeline sounds good, would like the bench spreadsheet by Monday.
[08:00] Maya: we'll aim for Monday. anything else?
[08:05] Sofia: one ask — include an example of routing policy in the doc so our platform folks can see rules.
[08:12] Ethan: will include a sample routing policy: route(product_widget) -> dedicated-low-latency; route(batch) -> dedicated-high-throughput; fallback -> hosted.
[08:25] Tom: last operational Q — SLA metrics, how do we monitor token-level cost?
[08:30] Maya: Redwood console gives token-level cost/latency per route and per token bucket, we can set alerts. we'll demo this in the latency POC.
[08:40] Priya: great, thanks.
[08:45] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll capture action items and follow up in the email.

End of transcript.
